## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{100}{0}{0}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_How can an agent remain controllable while its model and tools are busy?_

A trajectory can obey every tool contract and still spend its allowance without finishing. It can wait on a valid test job while an operator needs to pause it, or compete for service with a task whose user is waiting. None of these decisions can depend on the model reaching a convenient stopping point. The runtime needs a current account of what the trajectory is doing, what it may do next, and what it still owes for work already started. Keeping that account outside the model makes intervention possible without confusing a request to stop with proof that every effect has ended. The harness uses it to govern continuation across calls and waits. In the H·S·A lens, this supervision bounds horizon exposure while preserving the state and authority obligations that earlier actions created.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Design a runtime-owned trajectory record that tracks live plans, grants, consumption, and outstanding obligations
- Construct guarded lifecycle transitions that distinguish current observation eligibility from unresolved external effects
- Apply external control requests without dispatching incomplete output or mistaking cancellation for settlement
- Explain which resources asynchronous waiting releases and which remain owned by the trajectory
- Design an approval lifecycle with expiry, current-condition checks, and guarded dispatch or refusal
- Allocate shared service fairly while distinguishing provider quotas and capacity from trajectory budgets
- Enforce bounded-liability budget admission and choose ceilings using measured task outcomes and costs

:::

## From an Agent Loop to a Supervised Trajectory {#sec-vol3-controlplane-need}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_h.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator triad with the Horizon axis highlighted."}

*The horizon exposure, bounded by a harness that keeps control outside the model.*
:::

### The anatomy of an unmanaged loop {#sec-vol3-harness-unmanaged-loop}

The connection-pool repair has produced candidate `r18`, and a test job is still running against a fixed snapshot of that revision. An operator requests a pause for inspection. Meanwhile, an independent interactive task is waiting for service, and the repair trajectory is approaching its budget. The test job can finish correctly and the next model reply can be well formed, yet neither event answers whether the repair should continue now. That decision depends on the operator's request, current task state, shared capacity, and the allowance left after accounting for work already started.

A deliberately minimal implementation calls the model, dispatches its proposed tools, appends their replies, and repeats until the model ends its turn. Without separately accessible control state and admission checks, it has nowhere to apply the pause while the test runs or to withhold another paid call. The defect is not the `while` loop. A loop or coroutine can implement a harness; supervision requires explicit state and rules that every continuation path respects. @Fig-vol3-controlplane-arch sets that loop beside the same loop running inside a harness.

::: {#fig-vol3-controlplane-arch fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Prototype Loop vs. the Agent Harness**: Panel (a) runs the model's proposed call directly and keeps all state in the message list, so an outside request has nowhere to land, nothing bounds cumulative spend, and calls that policy would gate run at once. Panel (b) wraps the same loop in a harness whose trajectory record, guarded transitions, control and approval paths, and reserved budgets decide what is admitted. The model only proposes, and the tool layer settles the outcomes of admitted calls." fig-alt="Two stacked panels. The top panel shows a five-line while loop that calls a model, breaks on end_turn, runs the tool call, and appends the result, with comments reading no gate, no deadline and state lives only here, beside three boxes: cannot be stopped from outside, no ceiling on turns, tokens, or dollars, and gated calls run at once. The bottom panel shows a model box, a harness box, and a tools and sandbox box, joined by paired arrows labeled proposal and context, and admitted call and observation. The harness box lists trajectory record, guarded state transitions, control actions and approval gates, and budgets and ceilings."}

![](images/svg/fig-vol3-controlplane-arch.svg)

:::

Tool calling, containment, and security already manage responsibilities that span time, including job handles, workspace leases, credential expiry, and unresolved effects. The harness brings those responsibilities together for one trajectory. An operator needs a current status without reconstructing the transcript; a scheduler needs to distinguish waiting work from work eligible to run; a dispatch path needs current grants and remaining allowance. These decisions share a runtime-owned record. The model may receive budget information and may cooperate with a pause request, but enforcement must not depend on its response, as required by invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}).

::: {#dfn-agent-harness .callout-definition title="Agent harness"}

***Agent harness***\index{Agent harness!definition} is the runtime component that owns the agent loop for one trajectory, assembling each model call, interpreting the reply, deciding whether and when each proposed tool call is dispatched, and keeping the record through which outside components inspect, pause, bound, or stop continuation.

1. **Significance**: It keeps continuation decisions independent of model cooperation while preserving the grants, consumption, and outstanding work those decisions must respect.
2. **Distinction**: The tool layer mediates calls and tracks their outcomes, and the sandbox bounds execution under its policy. The harness composes those mechanisms with control requests, waiting, scheduling, and lifetime budgets.
3. **Common pitfall**: Keeping status and pending obligations only in prompt text or inaccessible execution-local state, so a separate control path cannot inspect them or prevent further dispatch.

:::

### One turn under supervision {#sec-vol3-harness-lifecycle-turn}

The repair job makes the division of labor concrete. @Tbl-vol3-harness-control-trace follows one illustrative event ordering, beginning with the model call that proposes the test. The state names describe whether continuation is eligible, running, waiting, or held; they do not enumerate every resource or prove that remote work has ended. The full record and its transition guards follow in the next sections.

| Event                                             | Harness decision and recorded obligation                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|:--------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| The repair is eligible for another model call     | From `READY`, check pending control, task conditions, shared admission, and remaining budget. Reserve the bounded call liability before entering `CALLING_MODEL` and dispatching the request                                        |
| A complete reply proposes the test of `r18`       | Reconcile reported model usage, preserving any unresolved charge. Validate the proposal and recheck control, authority, and budget before reserving tool liability and registering the operation for dispatch. Enter `WAITING_TOOL` |
| The operator requests a pause while the test runs | Hold new admission. Withdraw the old wait's eligibility to resume the model, retain the operation and its liabilities in the operation ledger, and pass through `READY` to `PAUSED` without a runnable gap                          |
| The test result arrives during the pause          | Authenticate and correlate it with the recorded operation and revision. Update outcome and usage evidence without resuming the old turn or automatically appending to a new context                                                 |
| The operator requests resume                      | Revalidate task state, grants, pending evidence, and allowance before returning to `READY`. The scheduler may then admit another call; the result supports only the test and revision it actually checked                           |

: **A repair trajectory under supervision**: An illustrative control trace, not a complete controller or a measured accuracy comparison. A paused trajectory does not admit new work, but its outstanding job and charges still require an owner. {#tbl-vol3-harness-control-trace}

The trace also exposes an accounting requirement. The next call must fit the allowance after accounting for outstanding work and the resources needed to finish; the amount already billed is not enough to make that decision. The budget section develops this reservation rule and its limits.

The same discipline applies when a reply contains several calls. The harness registers each admitted operation before its response can arrive and checks pending control before each dispatch; if admission stops midway, the record still accounts for the calls already started. A canceled or incomplete model reply supplies no dispatchable proposal. A model reply that requests completion initiates the task's final checks rather than proving success. Approval, when required by policy, adds an undispatched hold with its own expiry and current-condition checks.

While the repair is held, an independent interactive trajectory can compete for service without waiting for this model to yield voluntarily. That does not mean the repair has released its workspace, cached state, or remote job. Supervision separates the decision to continue from the resources and effects that remain owned. The record comes first because each of these decisions needs a current account of the trajectory; guarded states then determine how that account may change, before control actions, waits, approval, scheduling, and budgets give each decision its enforcement rule.

## The Trajectory Record {#sec-vol3-controlplane-acb}

The repair has dispatched a test of candidate r18 when the operator requests a pause. The next decision depends on more than the transcript: the test's status and candidate revision, the acknowledged control request, and the allowance remaining after outstanding work is accounted for. An independent interactive task also needs service, so the scheduler must distinguish a waiting repair from a trajectory eligible for its next model call. These decisions require runtime-owned control state that can be inspected without asking the model to reconstruct it.

::: {#dfn-trajectory-record .callout-definition title="Trajectory record"}

***Trajectory record***\index{Trajectory record!definition} is the per-trajectory control state owned by the harness: identity and task scope, lifecycle state, limits and accounting, grants and leases, pending work, and references to the context, live plan, workspace, and supporting evidence.

1. **Significance**: It gives the runtime an explicit place to inspect and govern the whole trajectory, including work and obligations that persist between model calls.
2. **Distinction**: The transcript records an interaction; the trajectory record governs its continuation. A live record is not by itself a durable history or proof that its recorded claims are true.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating a model-generated progress report as an authoritative update to spend, permissions, operation outcomes, or task completion.

:::

@Tbl-vol3-acb-schema groups fields by the decision they support. The groups describe a logical record, not a required memory layout or serialization format. A runtime can store some groups separately and retain references to them, provided their ownership and update rules remain explicit.

| Field group                         | Contents                                                                                                       | Supervisory use                                                                       |
|:------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Identity and task                   | Trajectory, requester, tenant, optional parent, task contract and version                                      | Bind requests and charges to the right task and authority                             |
| Control                             | `state`, `record_version`, `control_epoch`, `pending_control`, exit reason                                     | Decide whether a continuation or state change is current and permitted                |
| Continuation                        | Context reference and version, live-plan reference and revision, candidate workspace and evidence references   | Assemble the next call from the intended task state                                   |
| Limits and accounting               | Per-call limits, `actual_consumption`, `outstanding_reservations`, `finalization_reserve`, and `deadline`      | Check new liability against the remaining allowance and preserve funds for final work |
| Authority and resources             | Current grants, workspace leases, credential-broker references, resource owners                                | Check accessible operations and identify resources requiring release or transfer      |
| Current invocation and observations | `current_model_call`, `observation_eligible_calls`, attempt IDs, job handles, deadlines, and expected versions | Correlate events and decide which may inform the current continuation                 |
| Held approval                       | `held_approval`: exact proposal reference, applicable task and plan versions, approval status and expiry       | Keep a proposed action undispatched while its decision is pending                     |
| Outstanding obligations             | `operation_ledger` reference, unresolved outcomes and charges, settlement owner                                | Preserve responsibility after a timeout, plan revision, pause, or scheduling exit     |

: **Trajectory Record Fields**: Each field group supports a control decision; references preserve access to larger state without implying that the referenced resources are free or absent. {#tbl-vol3-acb-schema}

The outstanding-obligations group is distinct from observation eligibility. A call can cease to be eligible for direct insertion into the next model context while its external outcome remains unresolved. The operation ledger retains the logical operation identity, transport attempts, received evidence, and the component responsible for settlement. A `record_version` identifies each serialized record update; a `control_epoch` marks the continuation against which proposals and observations are checked. Changing that epoch does not create a new logical operation or authorize a repeat. @Sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency established the repeat contract; the harness must keep its obligations reachable even when the trajectory stops waiting for an observation.

The same separation applies to accounting. Actual consumption records established usage; outstanding reservations account for admitted work whose final charge is not yet settled. A protected finalization reserve covers the declared final checks and cleanup rather than remaining available for exploration. An elapsed-time deadline is separate: waiting consumes time even when no new model tokens are generated. @Sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting develops the admission and settlement rules; the record supplies the quantities those rules need.

### Govern updates and referenced state

The model does not write the control record directly. The harness can accept a model's proposed plan or completion claim, but applies it only through the relevant checks. Usage comes from the configured provider or tool accounting source, authenticated tool events supply operation evidence, and authorized control requests supply pause or cancellation intent. These inputs require correlation and validation; moving a value outside the prompt does not make it correct. The model may receive a remaining-budget notice without gaining permission to alter the meter.

Referencing the context, plan, and workspace avoids copying their contents into every status query. It does not reduce a waiting trajectory to a record alone. Its workspace, stored observations, open jobs, and unsettled requests may still consume resources. Serving-state retention belongs to @sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping, and workspace lifetime belongs to @sec-vol3-sandboxes-lease. The harness retains the relevant references and communicates its continuation needs without prescribing cache eviction or workspace destruction after every call.

This record is the live control representation. Keeping its history through host failure is the responsibility developed in @sec-vol3-durable-execution. A log reference can connect the two, but a pointer to a log does not itself establish crash-safe ordering or recoverability.

### Maintain a live plan {#sec-vol3-harness-live-plan}

@Sec-vol3-test-time-compute-planning-revision used dependencies to revise candidate artifacts. Once operations are admitted, the harness needs a live plan that also distinguishes proposed work from work already started and evidence already obtained. Each step has an identity, its prerequisite steps or evidence, the candidate and conditions to which it applies, and a recorded status. An admitted step links to its operation-ledger entry. A completed step links to the evidence supporting that status; a checked box in model output is not enough.

For the repair, the plan can distinguish the source edit producing candidate r18, the targeted check of that candidate, and the remaining checks required by the task. While the targeted job is outstanding, the plan records that wait rather than claiming a pass. When its result arrives, a passing observation supports only the recorded check under its recorded conditions. It does not mark every remaining step complete or establish acceptance of the whole repair. The operator's pause request remains a separate control event; it does not change the test's historical inputs or outcome.

The model can propose a plan revision when new evidence changes what work appears useful. The harness checks the revision against the current task, evidence dependencies, grants, and budget before adopting it. Adoption advances the plan revision and invalidates affected undispatched proposals and held approvals whose assumptions no longer match. Unaffected evidence can remain available under its original conditions. These changes must be coordinated with dispatch so that an old proposal cannot pass admission against a newly adopted plan.

Suppose a later revision proposes changing the source after r18's targeted check has been dispatched. The running check still concerns r18; relabeling the plan cannot turn its eventual result into evidence for the changed candidate. Nor does removing that step cancel the job, erase its possible effects, or refund its reservation. The harness retains the admitted operation and its settlement owner, withholds dependent work where its preconditions remain unresolved, and evaluates any replacement call as a new admission. Repairing effects already performed belongs to failure recovery, not to editing plan text.

The record now identifies what the trajectory proposes, what it has admitted, and what still requires attention. To make that description reliable under competing events, the harness must constrain how it changes. The next section gives its status field a closed set of meanings and guarded transitions.

## Trajectory States {#sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine}

The repair trajectory has submitted the tests for candidate `r18`. Its wait deadline passes before a result arrives, and the harness records that the outcome is unknown. A minute later, the test service reports success. These facts do not contradict each other: the first describes what was known at the deadline; the second adds evidence. The failure would be to insert that result into an obsolete turn as though it had been available when the model made its next decision. This **observation crossing**\index{Observation crossing} confuses the history of an operation with the evidence admitted to a particular continuation.

A state machine makes that admission explicit. It also prevents a scheduler from treating a trajectory held for approval as merely idle and starting another model call. The runtime, not generated text, owns the transitions. @Tbl-vol3-lifecycle-states defines one supervisory machine with six live states and three terminal outcomes. Its states describe the continuation's eligibility, not a complete inventory of resources or remote work.

| State                             | Meaning                                                                                  | Legal next states                                          |
|:----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|
| `READY`                           | Eligible to be considered for the next model call; admission guards still apply.         | `CALLING_MODEL`, `PAUSED`, `FINALIZING`                    |
| `CALLING_MODEL`                   | A model invocation is registered for the current continuation.                           | `READY`, `WAITING_TOOL`, `AWAITING_APPROVAL`, `FINALIZING` |
| `WAITING_TOOL`                    | The continuation awaits a declared set or batch of tool observations.                    | `READY`, `FINALIZING`                                      |
| `AWAITING_APPROVAL`               | An exact proposed action is held; approval and dispatch eligibility remain unresolved.   | `WAITING_TOOL`, `READY`, `FINALIZING`                      |
| `PAUSED`                          | The continuation is held at a local boundary; no new model or tool work is admitted.     | `READY`, `FINALIZING`                                      |
| `FINALIZING`                      | The runtime is checking the exit outcome and resolving or transferring remaining duties. | `COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, `CANCELED`                          |
| `COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, `CANCELED` | The continuation has ended; retained evidence and assigned obligations may remain.       | None                                                       |

: **Guarded Trajectory States**: An edge permits consideration of a transition, not unconditional execution. Events can update accounting or evidence without changing state. {#tbl-vol3-lifecycle-states}

The ordinary cycle is `READY` → `CALLING_MODEL` → `WAITING_TOOL` → `READY`, drawn with every guarded edge in @fig-vol3-harness-trajectory-states. A model response may instead produce no admissible action, request completion, or propose an action requiring approval. The normalized invocation status of @tbl-vol3-invocation-status already fixes what the runtime may do with each outcome; the harness adds where each outcome leaves the trajectory. A `COMPLETED` reply goes to candidate validation. A validated tool proposal enters `WAITING_TOOL` once its dispatch is admitted, or `AWAITING_APPROVAL` when policy requires review; a completion request enters `FINALIZING` for the task's completion check; a reply with no admissible action returns to `READY` with an observation. `TRUNCATED`, `REFUSED`, and `REJECTED` replies return to `READY` with a bounded observation unless the task's refusal policy finalizes. A `CANCELED` reply returns to `READY` under the control hold that caused it. `TRANSPORT_FAILURE` and `FAULTED` return to `READY` for bounded failure handling while the budget permits and enter `FINALIZING` otherwise; their reservations remain outstanding until usage settles. A malformed or canceled partial response cannot become a tool invocation merely because some arguments can be recovered from it. An approved action goes from `AWAITING_APPROVAL` to `WAITING_TOOL` only when its current dispatch guards pass; a recorded approval alone need not change the state. Denial, expiry, or withdrawal can return a refusal observation to `READY`. The approval section develops these cases.

::: {#fig-vol3-harness-trajectory-states fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Trajectory State Machine**: Six live states and three terminal outcomes. The ordinary cycle runs from READY through CALLING_MODEL and WAITING_TOOL back to READY; a proposal that policy requires reviewed is held in AWAITING_APPROVAL, and pause is entered only from READY. Every exit passes through FINALIZING, which stops admission and resolves or transfers remaining duties before an absorbing terminal state. Each arrow is a guarded edge, and events such as a late result or a usage report can update the record's ledger without changing state." fig-alt="State diagram with a live-states region and an exit region. Live states PAUSED, READY, CALLING_MODEL, WAITING_TOOL, and AWAITING_APPROVAL are connected by labeled arrows: pause and resume, call admitted, no admissible action, tool call admitted, approval required by policy, approved and guards pass, wait policy met, and a dashed arrow for denied, expired, or stale requests back to READY. A completion request arrow and a dashed arrow from any live state for cancel, kill, or a budget or deadline stop lead to FINALIZING, which leads to COMPLETED, FAILED, and CANCELED."}

![](images/svg/harness-trajectory-states.svg)

:::

### Guard the transition and its admission

A legal edge is only the first check. Moving from `READY` to `CALLING_MODEL` also requires no pending control hold, a current task and context, applicable grants, available service capacity, and sufficient reserved budget for the bounded invocation liability. Dispatching a tool adds checks for its complete arguments, current authority, dependencies, and any required exact-action approval. An unresolved earlier operation can block a dependent mutation even while the trajectory is `READY` for independent work. Budget admission must preserve the allowance needed for final checks and cleanup, not spend it on the next turn.

These checks and their local consequences form one serialized update of the runtime-owned record. Before releasing a request, the harness registers the invocation or operation attempt, reserves its liability, records its observation eligibility, and changes state. Otherwise a fast completion could arrive before the runtime knows which request it belongs to. Every supported event has an explicit guard; an absent guard is not permission. Repeated delivery of an event must not admit the same action twice.

The `record_version` detects competing updates. The `control_epoch` identifies the continuation against which proposals and observations were admitted; changing that continuation can make a previously eligible response obsolete. Neither replaces the logical operation ID or the transport attempt ID. A retry may create another attempt within one operation, whereas a control change can invalidate a response without undoing that operation.

Serialization applies to the local decision, not the duration of network I/O. The harness releases the record lock before calling a model or tool service. If an accepted pause wins the admission race, the later dispatch is refused. If dispatch admission wins first, a subsequent pause must account for already-admitted work, including a request whose transmission is underway. It cannot retrospectively establish that no request left the host. Tool-side conditions still require the enforcement described in @sec-vol3-tool-calling.

@Lst-vol3-guarded-transition expresses this contract as one function. The legal edges are exactly those of @tbl-vol3-lifecycle-states, and every edge has an explicit guard; an edge with no registered guard is refused rather than allowed by default. The caller passes the `record_version` it read when it made its decision, so a competing update fails the version check, and a repeated delivery of the same event fails either that check or the edge check, instead of admitting the action twice. Admission work runs inside the lock and network I/O runs after it.

::: {#lst-vol3-guarded-transition lst-cap="**Guarded Transitions**: Every state change checks the legal edge, its explicit guard, and the record version under the record lock, then performs admission bookkeeping before the state changes; the admitted request is sent only after the lock is released."}
```python
LIVE = {"READY", "CALLING_MODEL", "WAITING_TOOL",
        "AWAITING_APPROVAL", "PAUSED"}
LEGAL = {("READY", "CALLING_MODEL"), ("READY", "PAUSED"),
         ("CALLING_MODEL", "READY"), ("CALLING_MODEL", "WAITING_TOOL"),
         ("CALLING_MODEL", "AWAITING_APPROVAL"), ("WAITING_TOOL", "READY"),
         ("AWAITING_APPROVAL", "WAITING_TOOL"),
         ("AWAITING_APPROVAL", "READY"), ("PAUSED", "READY")}
LEGAL |= {(s, "FINALIZING") for s in LIVE}
LEGAL |= {("FINALIZING", t) for t in ("COMPLETED", "FAILED", "CANCELED")}
# GUARDS maps each edge to a predicate over (record, decision).

def transition(rec, new_state, decision, admit=None):
    with rec.lock:                            # the local decision only
        edge = (rec.state, new_state)
        guard = GUARDS.get(edge)              # no guard, no permission
        if edge not in LEGAL or guard is None or not guard(rec, decision):
            raise IllegalTransition(edge, decision.id)
        if decision.seen_version != rec.record_version:
            raise StaleDecision(decision.id)  # a competing update won
        if admit is not None:
            admit(rec)                        # reserve, register, set eligibility
        rec.state = new_state
        rec.record_version += 1
        rec.history.append((edge, decision.id, rec.record_version))
    # The caller sends any admitted request after the lock is released.
```
:::

The guard for `READY` → `CALLING_MODEL`, for example, tests pending control, task and context currency, grants, capacity, and the budget inequality developed in @sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting. The lock is held for a few lookups and an append, negligible beside a model call, so guarding every transition costs almost nothing.

This is a live-host coordination contract. It does not by itself make the record survive a crash or make a local update atomic with an external effect. @Sec-vol3-durable-execution develops the durable intent and recovery ordering needed across that boundary.

### Preserve outcomes without reviving an obsolete turn

The record separates `observation_eligible_calls` from the `operation_ledger`. The first identifies responses that may advance the current wait under its declared policy. The second retains admitted attempts, known outcomes, unresolved effects, charges, and the owner responsible for settlement. Removing a call from the eligibility set therefore does not remove its operation from the ledger.

On arrival, the runtime authenticates a result and correlates its task, logical operation, and attempt identity. It then records admissible outcome evidence in the ledger. A matching current response can also satisfy the wait policy and contribute an observation to the next context. A stale response cannot be appended directly to an obsolete turn, but it can still settle an outstanding operation. If that evidence matters to resumed work, the runtime revalidates its relevance and stages it during a subsequent guarded context assembly. Unknown or mismatched identities are not accepted as task evidence.

@Lst-vol3-harness-on-result shows the two paths. Ledger evidence and usage settlement happen for every authenticated, correlated result; staging an observation for the waiting continuation happens only when the call is still eligible under the current `control_epoch`. When the declared wait policy is satisfied, the return to `READY` goes through the ordinary guarded transition, whose guard evaluates that policy again under the lock.

::: {#lst-vol3-harness-on-result lst-cap="**Routing a Tool Result**: Authenticated evidence always reaches the operation ledger and settles usage, while only a currently eligible result under the current control epoch is staged for the waiting continuation."}
```python
def on_tool_result(rec, result):
    if not authenticate(result):
        return audit(rec, "unauthenticated_result", result)
    with rec.lock:
        op = rec.operation_ledger.get(result.operation_id)
        if op is None or result.attempt_id not in op.attempts:
            return audit(rec, "unknown_operation", result)
        if not op.record_evidence(result):  # already recorded: duplicate
            return
        settle(rec, op, result.usage)       # reserved -> actual; rest stays owed
        eligible = (result.call_id in rec.observation_eligible_calls
                    and result.epoch == rec.control_epoch)
        if eligible:
            rec.observation_eligible_calls.discard(result.call_id)
            stage_observation(rec, result)  # for the current wait only
        rec.record_version += 1
        seen = rec.record_version
    if eligible and wait_policy_satisfied(rec):  # the guard rechecks it
        transition(rec, "READY", Decision(result.id, seen))
```
:::

A stale result therefore settles its operation and charge without entering the obsolete turn, which closes the observation crossing while keeping the evidence that later settlement needs.

Returning from `WAITING_TOOL` to `READY` follows the declared wait policy: all required results, an allowed partial batch, a timeout, or an explicit withdrawal. The record distinguishes received evidence from unresolved members. In the repair example, a timeout cannot justify claiming that the `r18` tests failed, and a later success must retain the candidate and test scope it actually covers. Nor does timeout authorize a blind repeat of an operation. Dependent actions remain subject to their preconditions and repeat-safety contract.

### Pause the continuation, not the operation history

This machine enters `PAUSED` only from `READY`. To pause active work, the runtime first records `pending_control`, preventing new admission. It withdraws the active model response's eligibility, withdraws any held approval, and closes the current observation wait as needed. It may request cancellation of admitted work, but unconfirmed cancellation remains unresolved in the operation ledger. Partial model output is retained only if useful for diagnostics, never repaired into a dispatchable call.

With those local eligibility decisions recorded, the runtime passes through `READY` to `PAUSED` under the same admission hold. There is no runnable interval between the two transitions. Reaching this boundary means no current response or held proposal can advance the continuation; it does not mean all tools have stopped. In particular, the outstanding `r18` test can finish while the trajectory is paused. Its result updates the owned ledger without automatically restarting the model.

Resume is a guarded `PAUSED` → `READY` transition. It rechecks the task, current grants, budget, context dependencies, and pending evidence. A withdrawn approval is not silently reused, and an unresolved operation still constrains dependent dispatch. Resource retention is separate: workspace leases, result buffers, reservations, or serving caches may remain under their respective lifetime policies. A paused trajectory is neither necessarily resource-free nor evidence that external effects were undone.

### Finalize with an explicit owner for remaining duties

Every exit passes through `FINALIZING`. The runtime stops ordinary work admission, records the exit reason, withdraws unused authority where supported, and applies the task's completion check when completion is claimed. The model's end-of-turn marker requests that check; it is not evidence that the repair works. Final checks and required cleanup use their funded allowance.

Finalization may wait for outcomes, fail to establish completion, or transfer unresolved cancellation, reconciliation, and charging duties to an explicitly accepting supervisor or service. The terminal transition requires those duties to be resolved or assigned, not merely deleted from a pending set. A transfer records enough identity, evidence, and resources for its owner to continue; changing a field to “transferred” without an owner does not satisfy the guard.

Terminal states are absorbing for the continuation. Late evidence can update retained records through its assigned owner, but cannot return the trajectory to `READY`. Starting work after a terminal outcome requires a new trajectory identity linked to the previous one; transport retries during an active trajectory do not universally require a new trajectory. `COMPLETED` records that the configured completion check passed. Whether that check is sufficient to count the task as accepted remains the evaluation question developed in @sec-vol3-evaluation.

::: {#chk-10-agent-control-block .callout-checkpoint title="Trajectory record and guarded states"}

- [ ] **Late test evidence**: The wait for `r18` times out, then a success result arrives during `PAUSED`. Which record may change, and what must happen before the next model call uses the result?
- [ ] **Pause boundary**: How can `WAITING_TOOL` pass through `READY` to `PAUSED` without permitting another call or claiming that the tool stopped?
- [ ] **Admission race**: Why must request identity and reserved liability be recorded before network dispatch, while network I/O stays outside the record lock?
- [ ] **Terminal responsibility**: What must remain owned if cancellation is unconfirmed when the continuation ends?

:::

The machine defines which changes are permitted and what each must preserve. Control actions now determine who can request those changes and how the runtime enforces them while work is active.

## Control Actions {#sec-vol3-controlplane-signals}

The test job for candidate `r18` is still outstanding when an operator requests a pause. The harness must stop the repair's continuation without losing the job's identity, its budget reservation, or the evidence it may return. Waiting for the test to finish before recording the request leaves the operator without control. Declaring the job canceled merely because the trajectory now says `PAUSED` invents an outcome the runtime has not observed.

Control separates the arrival of a request from the conditions it establishes. The harness authenticates the requester, checks authority over this trajectory, and records the requested action in `pending_control` through the same serialized control path that guards dispatch. A pause or cancellation closes admission to new model calls and tool operations before the controller acknowledges that hold. An operation already admitted remains owned work. The response to the operator must distinguish “request received,” “new admission stopped,” and any later confirmation that running work terminated.

### Admission boundaries and active generation

A **turn boundary**\index{Turn boundary} is a point at which the harness can decide whether continuation is still permitted before admitting its next operation. It occurs before a model invocation and before tool dispatch, including dispatch of each separately admitted call in a proposed batch. The control check and admission decision must share concurrency protection; checking a flag and then dispatching outside that protection can let a pause arrive between the two. Registering an admitted operation before dispatch also ensures that a fast reply finds its owner.

The boundary is a local admission guarantee, not a claim that every remote operation has ended. If the control request wins the ordering, the next operation is withheld. If dispatch admission wins, the controller treats the operation as outstanding and applies the appropriate cancellation or completion policy. This distinction makes the remaining obligation inspectable instead of hiding it behind the timestamp of a stop button.

Generation need not finish before local candidate processing stops. The harness can request streaming cancellation\index{Streaming cancellation}, close the invocation's eligibility to produce an actionable candidate, and retain partial content only for bounded diagnosis. The invocation contract in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract governs the result. A canceled or truncated payload cannot become a dispatchable call because a parser closes its brackets, because its prefix already parses, or because a complete-looking reply arrives after its eligibility was withdrawn; the quarantining invariant (principle \ref{pri-02-quarantining-invariant}) holds regardless of how the invocation ended. Such late evidence can still settle usage or explain what the service did.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-harness-boundary-wait
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TIME TO THE NEXT TURN BOUNDARY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-controlplane-signals, "Output and time limits" paragraph.
# │ Goal: Show how long one admitted call can hold off the next turn boundary.
# │ Show: Reference per-token output allowance, a scenario output ceiling,
# │       and their product.
# │ How: Same registry path as the foundation-model cost cell: 8-bit weight
# │      bytes / accelerator bandwidth per generated token. No queueing,
# │      stalls, or serving overhead, so the product understates real waits.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_time

class BoundaryWait:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    weight_bytes = BYTES_INT8
    k_max = 4_096  # scenario: per-call output-token allowance

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = model.parameters / ureg.param * weight_bytes
    t_dec = (weights / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    t_wait = (k_max * t_dec).to(second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(60 * second < t_wait < 120 * second, "Boundary wait exceeds one minute")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_dec_ms_str = fmt_time(t_dec, unit=ms, precision=3)
    k_max_str = fmt_count(k_max)
    t_wait_str = fmt_time(t_wait, unit=second, precision=1)
```

Output and time limits perform different jobs. A service-enforced output allowance bounds the generated quantity under that service's accounting contract. It does not bound elapsed time without further assumptions about queueing, stalls, and generation rate. Even under the most favorable of those assumptions, the wait is long. At the reference output allowance of `{python} BoundaryWait.t_dec_ms_str` per generated token from @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost, with no queueing or stall, a call admitted with a `{python} BoundaryWait.k_max_str`-token output allowance can hold the next turn boundary about `{python} BoundaryWait.t_wait_str` away. A pending cancel or pause that waited for the reply to end would wait at least that long, which is why the harness needs streaming cancellation rather than turn boundaries alone. A host deadline determines when the supervisor stops waiting and initiates intervention; neither that deadline nor a closed stream proves that remote inference stopped. Reported final usage settles the reservation. Missing usage remains an outstanding liability rather than an assumed refund.

### Pause and resume under one policy

The guarded pause path established in @sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine holds admission while passing through `READY` to `PAUSED`. Its operator-facing meaning depends on the policy for already admitted work. For the `r18` test, the policy may allow the job to finish under its existing limits while holding the repair's continuation. A policy requiring the job to stop instead requests cancellation and records what the executor confirms. A pause that permits execution to continue is not a frozen workspace and must not be presented as one. Inspection requiring quiescence needs confirmation that the relevant writers have stopped or an isolated snapshot with a declared boundary.

Resume is another guarded request, not the inverse of every action taken during pause. The harness reconciles pending evidence, checks the current task and grants, and verifies that the remaining budget and deadline permit continuation. Expired credentials do not become valid again; withdrawn approvals do not revive; an abandoned partial reply does not resume halfway through its arguments. A usable continuation returns to `READY` for ordinary admission. If unresolved effects invalidate a proposed mutation's preconditions, that mutation remains withheld even when independent work is eligible.

@Tbl-vol3-signal-vocabulary compares the requested changes to continuation. The final column names the supervisory outcome, not proof that all external work has stopped.

| Request                         | Required control effect                                                            | Guarded outcome                                                              |
|:--------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Cancel                          | Hold new admission; request cancellation and account for owned work                | `FINALIZING`, then a recorded cancellation outcome when finalization permits |
| Interrupt with new instructions | Hold affected proposals; validate the instruction and revise its task dependencies | `READY` only when the revised continuation is eligible                       |
| Pause                           | Hold continuation and preserve an owner for outstanding work                       | `READY` to `PAUSED` with no runnable gap                                     |
| Resume                          | Reconcile evidence and recheck current permission and limits                       | `PAUSED` to `READY`, or remain held if guards fail                           |
| Kill                            | Stop admission and invoke available enforcement against active work                | `FINALIZING`, with confirmed and unresolved outcomes recorded                |
| Budget or deadline stop         | Deny further ordinary admission; preserve funded finalization duties               | `FINALIZING`, with the stopping reason and remaining obligations             |

: **Control requests and their enforced scope**: A control action changes admission and continuation through the guarded lifecycle. Cancellation and termination of already admitted work require separate evidence. {#tbl-vol3-signal-vocabulary tbl-colwidths="[22,41,37]"}

A new user instruction also needs this discipline. Adding “change the target file instead” to the next prompt does not invalidate a previously admitted edit or update the scope of an existing approval. The harness records the instruction, determines which plan steps and proposals it supersedes, and checks whether outstanding operations conflict with the revised task. It cannot erase their possible effects by replacing the plan text.

### Termination and remaining obligations

Kill requests invoke enforcement without waiting for model cooperation or a completed reply, as out-of-band preemption requires (principle \ref{pri-vol3-preemptive-interrupts}). The controller can stop local execution, revoke mediated access, or fence obsolete workers on the paths its execution boundary controls. The sandbox lifetime contract in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling-reset determines which processes, descendants, channels, and resources that enforcement covers. Terminating one process does not certify that all remote work ended, and changing a grant field does not close an already usable handle.

Finalization therefore records confirmed termination separately from unresolved effects and charges. It may wait for evidence, fail cleanup, or transfer a remaining obligation to an identified settlement owner. The operation's repeat contract, established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency, determines whether another attempt is safe, and settlement comes before any retry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}); an identifier alone cannot answer what the interrupted attempt did. Even a terminal scheduling state must not cause the runtime to discard evidence that could settle that obligation.

Outside control makes continuation independent of the model's willingness to cooperate. It does not require a worker to remain occupied while a job or cancellation response is outstanding. The next design step is to preserve these control and evidence obligations while the trajectory waits, then admit continuation only when the appropriate event and guards allow it.

## Waiting Without Losing Supervision {#sec-vol3-controlplane-yielding}

The repair trajectory has dispatched a test job for candidate `r18`. While the test runs, an operator requests a pause and an independent interactive task becomes ready for service. The repair needs no new model output merely to remain aware of these events. It does need a supervisor that can find the job, hold continuation, and retain its eventual evidence without depending on a worker blocked inside the test call.

An asynchronous wait releases the worker to handle other work while the trajectory record identifies what remains pending. A blocking implementation can also remain controllable if an independent supervisor handles control requests and deadlines. The design requirement is therefore not a particular event-loop library. Waiting must leave the control record accessible, and a returning event must pass through that record's guards before it can advance the trajectory.

### From an event to an eligible observation

The job interface in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-async already distinguishes acceptance from completion. The harness composes that interface with its lifecycle. Before a dispatched job can return evidence, the runtime registers its owning trajectory, call and attempt identities, job handle when available, expected source revision, observation eligibility, and outstanding liability. Registration and dispatch bookkeeping must account for a result that arrives immediately. A notification must never outrun the record needed to interpret it.

@Tbl-vol3-event-wakeup-pipeline follows a result through the supervisor. These are logical obligations, not a prescription for a kernel reactor or one thread per stage.

| Stage                        | Harness responsibility                                                                                                                                                  | What does not follow automatically                                          |
|:-----------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Receive an event             | Obtain a notification, status reply, timer event, or control request through the designated interface.                                                                  | A notification establishes a completed result.                              |
| Authenticate and correlate   | Check the source and match the event to its task, operation or attempt, and recorded execution context.                                                                 | A matching identifier authorizes a new action or makes the payload true.    |
| Update the record            | Preserve reported outcome, source revision, capture limits, usage, and any unresolved obligation; decide whether the evidence is eligible for the waiting continuation. | Evidence for an earlier attempt belongs directly in the current model turn. |
| Apply the continuation guard | Evaluate pending controls, the wait policy, dependencies, current grants, and budget before making continuation eligible.                                               | New evidence requires an immediate model call.                              |

: **Event handling before continuation**: Receiving evidence, recording its meaning, and admitting further work are separate supervisory decisions. {#tbl-vol3-event-wakeup-pipeline tbl-colwidths="[20,43,37]"}

The event handler updates the record under the same concurrency discipline as the state machine, checking its `record_version` and the continuation's `control_epoch`. A repeated notification must not append the observation twice, charge reported usage twice, or enqueue duplicate continuation. Membership in `observation_eligible_calls` governs admission to the waiting continuation; the separate `operation_ledger` retains outstanding effects and liabilities. An older epoch prevents direct append to an obsolete model turn, but authenticated evidence about that operation still goes to its settlement owner. Any use in the current continuation requires fresh validation and staging. Correlation protects which record receives evidence; the tool's result contract determines what that evidence establishes.

The same distinction applies to streamed output. A log fragment or progress event can update a bounded observation store without ending the wait. An opening tool-call delimiter in a model stream is not a completed proposal and cannot trigger dispatch. Model invocation completion and validation remain the adapter's responsibility, while the harness determines whether a completed proposal is still eligible under the current control state.

### Waiting for a job or a batch

For a long-running job, the harness can await a notification or obtain status through bounded runtime polling. Neither requires asking the model repeatedly whether to keep waiting. An explicit request for additional input may justify a new decision, but forwarding that input is another authorized operation. The record preserves the job's state and pending input requirement rather than treating every output line as permission to resume.

A batch needs a declared continuation policy. Under an all-results policy, the harness waits until every member has either supplied the required result or reached a defined waiting disposition, such as a timeout with its effect still unresolved. A partial-results policy may allow independent reasoning after one result arrives, while other calls remain outstanding. It must preserve which evidence is missing and prevent a dependent action from proceeding as though the whole batch had completed. The transition to `READY` expresses eligibility for the permitted continuation, not proof that the trajectory owns no unfinished work.

For example, a completed lint result need not settle a concurrent test job. If the next decision requires both checks on `r18`, receiving lint output alone does not satisfy the wait policy. If the next decision is an independent inspection, a partial-results policy can admit it under the current limits. Editing the candidate while the test reads a mutable workspace would require additional coordination; merely labeling the work parallel does not preserve the tested revision.

A deadline ends the specified wait, not necessarily the operation. The harness records the timeout, requests the defined intervention, and changes observation eligibility without deleting the unresolved effect or charge. A later success is new evidence about that operation, not a contradiction of the earlier timeout. The settlement contract in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency determines whether the evidence resolves the outcome and whether repetition is safe. Removing a call from the current wait set cannot provide that guarantee.

### A result arriving during a pause

Return to the test job and the operator's pause request. The admission hold prevents new work while the harness follows the guarded path through `READY` to `PAUSED`, without making the trajectory briefly runnable between those states. The record retains the job and any unresolved effects or charges under an explicit owner. Pausing continuation does not require pretending that the test has stopped.

If the test result then arrives, the supervisor can authenticate it, match it to the `r18` job, and record its outcome while leaving the trajectory `PAUSED`. A targeted `test_waiter_notified_on_return` pass remains evidence for that test and revision, not acceptance of the full repair. The event does not override the operator's hold. On an authorized resume, the harness rechecks current control state, grants, budget, and accumulated evidence before deciding which continuation is eligible. If the deadline or budget prevents further work, receiving a useful result does not create a fresh allowance.

The event processor therefore remains active while model continuation is held. The same principle applies during finalization: evidence can update an owned outstanding obligation without reviving a terminal trajectory. Crash-safe preservation of those obligations is the additional problem developed in @sec-vol3-durable-execution.

### Account for what the wait retains

Releasing a worker does not release the test process, workspace, captured output, network connection, or retained inference state. The record references these resources and their owners. Storage and tool charges may continue, reservations remain until their liabilities are settled, and the elapsed task deadline continues advancing. Status polling and cleanup also consume resources and need to fit the applicable limits.

The workspace lease preserves candidate edits and test artifacts under the lifetime contract of @sec-vol3-sandboxes-lease. It is not automatically destroyed and recreated at every tool boundary. The serving policy separately decides whether compatible KV state is kept, moved, or dropped, using the trade-offs in @sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping. The harness can supply an expected wait and resumption requirements, but a deadline is not a prediction of completion, and a hosted service may not expose cache-placement controls.

A wait is thus a supervised interval with retained evidence, resources, and obligations. Its end makes some continuation eligible only when the record's guards permit it. Approval uses the same discipline for a different dependency: the operation has not yet been dispatched, and continuation awaits an authorized decision that may arrive late, be denied, or expire.

## Approval Gates {#sec-vol3-controlplane-hitl}

The internal-review example in @sec-vol3-security-credentials permits submitting candidate `r18` and selected check records only after an authorized reviewer agrees. The proposal is complete, but the reviewer is unavailable. Meanwhile, the task's deadline continues to advance, an operator can request a pause, and the source or grant can change. The harness must hold the proposed submission without allowing a retry path or another model call to dispatch it while review remains unresolved.

::: {#dfn-escrow .callout-definition title="Approval escrow"}

***Approval escrow***\index{Escrow!definition}\index{Approval gate!escrow} is the harness's retention of an undispatched proposal pending required approval or subsequent dispatch admission. The held record binds the proposal to its task, approval conditions, and expiry; a favorable decision still requires current admission checks before execution.

1. **Significance**: It separates proposing an operation from permission to execute it now, while keeping the wait visible to outside control.
2. **Distinction**: Authorization establishes who may approve which represented action. The harness manages the lifetime of that pending decision and its transition to refusal or dispatch.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating a recorded approval as an unconditional instruction to execute, even after the proposal, grants, deadline, or relevant environment state has changed.

:::

Review is a task-policy choice, not a consequence of every irreversible operation. Some actions are prohibited outright; others can proceed under a sufficiently narrow automated policy. A disclosure or reversible mutation may also require review. The gate therefore follows trusted policy over the actual operation, target, and data scope rather than the model's characterization of the action as safe. Requesting review cannot enlarge a grant the reviewer has no authority to change.

The gate should also stay narrow. A reviewer asked to approve dozens of routine calls an hour learns to approve without reading, and a gate that always approves supplies no closure. Grants, sandboxes, and automated policy handle the operations they can make safe, which reserves review for the operations they cannot. The narrower the gate, the more each approval reflects an actual reading of the held proposal.

### Hold an identifiable proposal

After validating a completed model response, the harness records the held proposal before publishing its approval request. The record references the task and requester, intended tool origin and operation, immutable candidate artifact and selected evidence, applicable preconditions, required approver policy, and approval expiry. It also assigns an approval-request identifier and a held-proposal version, and computes the approval digest\index{Approval digest}, a hash of the canonical held proposal covering the operation, its arguments, its target, and the versions of the referenced artifacts. The approval binds to that digest, as in @sec-vol3-security-credentials, so changing any argument or artifact produces a different digest and voids the approval. These identifiers and the digest identify the decision under review; they are not the logical operation or transport-attempt identities used after dispatch.

For the review submission, the held artifact is the exact `r18` patch and named check records, not a path whose contents can change before use. The selected records retain their evidential scope; a targeted test pass does not become full acceptance because it appears in an approval request. The authentication and represented-action requirements are those already established in @sec-vol3-security-credentials. The harness adds the recorded status needed to distinguish pending, denied, expired, withdrawn, and admitted requests. @Fig-vol3-human-escrow shows the held request for this submission and the gate that resolves it.

::: {#fig-vol3-human-escrow fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Approval Gate**: Panel (a) lists what the reviewer approves for the r18 review submission: the exact proposal, its destination and data scope, the selected evidence with its limited scope, the preconditions, the digest that binds the approval, the expiry, and the requesting trajectory. Panel (b) holds the proposal without sending it, obtains a decision the model takes no part in, and rechecks current conditions at the dispatch boundary. An approval without capacity stays held; a denial, expiry, or stale proposal returns a refusal observation." fig-alt="Two panels. The left panel lists seven boxes: an exact proposal showing a submit_review call for revision r18 with an immutable patch and named check records, destination and data scope, selected evidence and its scope, preconditions, approval digest, expiry, and requesting trajectory. The right panel shows four numbered steps connected by downward arrows, hold the proposal, send the request to an authorized reviewer, decision, and re-check at the dispatch boundary, branching into three boxes: approved and current, which enters WAITING_TOOL; approved with no capacity, which remains in AWAITING_APPROVAL; and denied, expired, or stale, which returns to READY if continuation is permitted."}

![](images/svg/fig-vol3-human-escrow.svg)

:::

The trajectory enters `AWAITING_APPROVAL` without sending the held tool call. Waiting releases its worker and requires no model inference merely to ask whether a person has answered. It still retains the proposal and referenced artifacts, and may retain a workspace lease or other resources. Their retention costs remain governed by the task. Under stable flow, Little's law (@sec-vol3-kv-workload-dynamics) makes the mean number of trajectories held in `AWAITING_APPROVAL` equal to the rate of approval requests multiplied by the mean time to a decision, so review latency, not model speed, sets how many held trajectories and retained resources the system carries. The approval expiry bounds this wait for a decision; the trajectory's elapsed-time deadline continues independently. Waiting is not a refund of elapsed time or of charges from previously admitted work.

### Resolve the wait without dispatching twice

The approval service returns an authenticated decision associated with the held request and its version. The harness checks the decision and its digest against the current record, rather than treating any approval message as permission to resume. Repeated delivery records no second decision or dispatch. A decision for a withdrawn, expired, or replaced request remains evidence about that earlier request and cannot revive it.

@Tbl-vol3-escrow-transitions distinguishes recording a decision from admitting the operation. The state remains a supervisory state, not a claim that all other resources or effect obligations have disappeared.

| Event while in `AWAITING_APPROVAL`                            | Recorded handling                                                                    | Continuation                                             |
|:--------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| Required decision has not arrived                             | Keep the proposal undispatched until its expiry or another control event             | Remain `AWAITING_APPROVAL`                               |
| Valid approval arrives, but capacity is unavailable           | Record the decision; retain the held request without dispatch                        | Remain `AWAITING_APPROVAL`; recheck at admission         |
| Reviewer denies, request expires, or proposal becomes stale   | Close the held request and record the specific refusal reason                        | Return to `READY` only if continuation remains permitted |
| Approval is valid and every current admission condition holds | Consume the held request for dispatch, reserve liability, and register the operation | Enter `WAITING_TOOL` and issue the admitted request      |
| Task deadline or terminating control takes precedence         | Withdraw any still-undispatched request and record the stop reason                   | Enter `FINALIZING`                                       |

: **Approval decisions and admission**: A favorable decision does not bypass current conditions or allocate execution capacity by itself. {#tbl-vol3-escrow-transitions}

Silence leaves the request unapproved; at expiry the runtime records an expired request, not a human denial. Both prevent dispatch, but the distinction matters when explaining the outcome. If continuation is still permitted, a bounded observation can state that the held operation was not sent:

```json
{"approval_id": "review_r18",
 "status": "REFUSED", "reason": "APPROVAL_EXPIRED",
 "dispatch_status": "not_sent"}
```

The next permitted model call can use this observation to propose a different course. It cannot extend the old approval's validity by asking again. A fresh request requires a current proposal and another policy decision; automated repeated requests should not turn a refusal into pressure on the reviewer. When a task deadline prevents another model call, the harness retains the refusal in the final record instead of spending resources to narrate it.

### Recheck at the dispatch boundary

A favorable decision may arrive while the review target has changed or the task is nearly out of budget. Before admission, the harness verifies the held artifact and decision, current grants, approval expiry, task deadline, pending controls, and relevant preconditions. It must also fit the proposed operation's bounded liability alongside actual consumption, outstanding reservations, and funded final checks or cleanup. A valid approval does not authorize an unaffordable operation. An admission refusal records its reason; a task-wide stopping condition routes to finalization. Capacity and rate-limit admission can delay execution, so checks made when the decision arrived are not sufficient for a later dispatch.

For example, the approved submission may depend on an unchanged target branch. An earlier read of that branch cannot exclude a change between the read and the submission. Where the action requires that condition, the endpoint must enforce the expected version together with its operation, or the system must provide an equivalent exclusion mechanism. Without that support, the harness cannot promise the approved precondition holds merely because it reread the branch shortly before sending. The conditional-operation contract belongs to @sec-vol3-tool-calling-schemas.

Concurrent approval, expiry, and control events must have a consistent admission order. Under the record's concurrency guard, the harness confirms that the held request is still eligible, commits its budget reservation, marks that request as consumed for dispatch, registers the operation and attempt identities, and enters `WAITING_TOOL`. It registers the work before issuing the external request so an immediate result can be correlated. The network operation proceeds outside the record lock. This is a live-host coordination rule; the crash-safe ordering of the record and external effect is developed in @sec-vol3-durable-execution.

The admission boundary also determines how a competing stop request is handled. A stop recorded before admission prevents that dispatch. If admission has already committed, the runtime must treat the operation as admitted work and invoke the applicable cancellation or settlement path, not report an undispatched refusal without evidence. A transport failure after the request may have left the host preserves an unknown effect under @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency. A consumed approval prevents a second local approval handler from sending again; it does not establish endpoint deduplication or settle a missing reply.

### Pause or withdraw a held request

A pause must preserve the state-machine contract from @sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine. Under the READY-boundary pause policy, the harness withdraws the still-held request, records that it was not dispatched, and reaches `READY` with new admission inhibited by the pending pause. It then enters `PAUSED` through the ordinary guard. A late approval for the withdrawn request cannot dispatch while paused or after resumption. Resuming rechecks the task's grants, deadline, budget, and retained evidence; if the action is still needed, it requires a current approval request.

Cancellation and task expiry instead route through `FINALIZING`, which retains any obligations from earlier dispatched work. Withdrawing the held review submission does not cancel an unrelated test job, settle its charges, or reverse its effects. The record makes those distinctions visible even though the proposed submission itself never left escrow.

::: {#chk-10-supervisory-state-machine .callout-checkpoint title="Approval over time"}

The internal-review submission for `r18` is held while the task approaches its deadline.

- [ ] A valid approval arrives while execution capacity is unavailable. Why does recording that decision not permit dispatch after expiry?
- [ ] An operator pauses the trajectory before admission, then the approval arrives. Which record prevents the withdrawn request from running after resume?
- [ ] The target branch changes after a pre-dispatch read. Which endpoint condition is needed to preserve the approved operation's precondition?
- [ ] Dispatch may have occurred before its reply was lost. Why is `dispatch_status: not_sent` now unjustified, and which outstanding records must remain?

:::

The approval gate now has a bounded lifetime and an explicit handoff from held proposal to admitted work. Human agreement is one condition in that handoff, alongside current authority, resource bounds, and action-time preconditions. Multiple trajectories can satisfy those conditions while competing for the same execution capacity, so the harness next needs a policy for sharing that capacity without bypassing their individual gates.

## Scheduling Concurrent Trajectories {#sec-vol3-controlplane-scheduling}

The repair trajectory is waiting for the targeted test of candidate `r18`. Meanwhile, an independent interactive task and a queue of maintenance tasks are ready to call the model. When the test result makes the repair eligible to continue, it joins that competition. Running whichever trajectory asks most often rewards aggressive retrying; always serving interactive work first can leave maintenance waiting indefinitely. The harness needs a policy for choosing among eligible calls, not just a way to launch them concurrently.

The admission unit here is a `READY` trajectory's **next model call**, not its entire remaining task or the tool execution that the reply may propose. `WAITING_TOOL`, `AWAITING_APPROVAL`, and `PAUSED` trajectories are not candidates for this queue. Completing a wait makes a trajectory eligible only through the guarded transition already established; it does not bypass scheduling. The serving engine then schedules the admitted request's computation. Its batching and cache allocation remain separate from the harness's choice of which task may submit work.

### Fair sharing needs a declared unit

Equal numbers of calls need not mean equal service. One maintenance call can carry a much longer prompt than an interactive call. A scheduler must therefore state what its shares measure. A simple policy charges each admitted call its full input-token count plus its allowed output-token count. This is a deliberately conservative *scheduling charge*: it measures admitted token allowance, not actual output, dollars, accelerator time, or task value. Cached input remains part of this charge. Another policy can use measured service, but then it needs an estimate at admission and a rule for reconciling that estimate afterward.

Weighted deficit round-robin offers one way to share the declared charge. Keep a queue and a credit counter for each service class, with a rotating queue of trajectories inside each class. Each round adds a quantum proportional to the class's weight. Admit calls from that class while their charges fit its remaining credit and the other gates permit; each admission deducts its charge. Then rotate to the next class. Unspent credit carries into later rounds so a larger admissible call can eventually fit. When a class has no eligible work, reset its credit. This adapts the credit-carryover mechanism of deficit round-robin [@shreedhar1995efficient] to model-call admission rather than packet transmission.

Credit belongs to the class in this policy, not to each trajectory. Opening many trajectories therefore does not multiply the class's share. Rotation within the class also matters: restarting every scheduler pass at the same first record can starve records later in the list. Limit admitted request size, give every class intended to make progress a positive weight, and retain the rotation position between passes. If credit is capped, its cap must accommodate the largest request the policy allows. Otherwise a large call can wait forever despite repeated replenishment.

These rules provide a service-sharing policy, not a wall-clock response guarantee. Credit cannot make an unavailable provider or a saturated resource run a call. A continuously overloaded workload needs admission limits on incoming tasks or an explicit rejection policy; adding priority does not create capacity.

### Quotas and capacity are separate gates

The call selected by the fairness policy must also fit the provider's request and token quotas. Their accounting contract determines what to reserve: input tokens, output allowance or reported output, cached input, and the relevant time window need not be treated identically. A cache discount on the bill does not establish a discount against a rate limit. Nor does a token quota specify how many requests may be in flight at once.

A local rate limiter can hold calls before dispatch rather than repeatedly discovering overload through rejection. It must account for the traffic sharing the same provider allocation, including other harness processes where applicable. A token bucket is suitable only to the extent that its burst and refill behavior match the allocation being enforced. Headroom and feedback from rejection or quota reports remain useful when the provider's window or competing traffic is not fully observable. No local bucket guarantees acceptance under an unknown shared limit.

Local resources impose further gates. A test job can need a bounded number of execution slots, memory, CPU service, and storage capacity even when model-request quota is plentiful. Use the units of the resource being limited: bytes of retained storage differ from bytes per second of transfer, and I/O operations per second differ from either. A count of identical sandbox slots can be useful under a declared per-slot resource envelope; a count alone does not bound heterogeneous jobs' memory use.

Workspace ownership follows @sec-vol3-sandboxes, not a universal acquire-and-destroy rule for every call. The repair may retain files between model calls while releasing a tool execution slot after a test ends. Those retained resources still count against capacity. Reserving some execution capacity for interactive work can protect that class from batch occupancy of the reserved pool, at the cost of unused capacity when there is no interactive demand. It does not remove contention on a different shared resource or preempt a job already running.

An approved tool call needs its own dispatch admission. If no suitable tool slot is available, the held action remains in `AWAITING_APPROVAL` with its recorded decision; it does not return to `READY` for another model call. A tool-dispatch queue can apply its own fair-sharing policy in meaningful units.
